title: A Slab soundtrack driven by the tracks and the camera
body:
@mrsarac pls also see #2 

A second, optional soundtrack for the video, made in [Slab](https://github.com/nooga/slab), a macOS DAW whose instruments and effects are code. `tools/render.sh` and `tools/sfx.py` are untouched.

It's darker and heavier than `sfx.py`: 120 BPM in F minor, so every 0.5 s cut lands on a beat. It reads the same `out/tracks.json`, and every hit sits on its frame:
- a kick and a bit-crushed noise burst on each cut
- a crushed tick per keystroke
- two electronic blips per lock (one per red frame) on random notes of F minor
- a rolling reese bass and a pad running Fm9 → Dbmaj7#11 → Eb6/9 → C7b9
- through the collapse: a kick roll, a glitch stutter and a two-octave bass dive
- on `Done`: a boom, an Fm(add9) chord and a bell

A transformer hum on worn tape runs underneath. The bass changes saturation on every shot (tube, tape, transformer, diode, fuzz, rail, valve, fold), level-matched. The whole mix drops to a crushed sampler (6 down to 3 bits) for the "— composing" shot. Everything below 30 Hz is cut. The result is about -10.7 LUFS with a -1 dBTP true peak.

**The camera drives the mix.** A new hud binary, `camera`, writes `out/camera.json`. The score uses it so that:
- the tracked box's position in the output pans the lock blips and keystrokes
- the filmed screen's slide across the frame pans the pad, riser, glitches, hum and echoes
- each shot's zoom push opens the bass filter and brightens the hats
- the two red lock frames crush the bass and the pad, the way the image tears

## How it was made

### Slab in one paragraph

Slab is a DAW: an arrangement of tracks with clips of notes, a mixer with buses and sends, automation lanes, and a headless renderer (`slab project.slab --render out.wav`). The host is written in Zig. Every instrument and effect ("machine") is written in fy, a small concatenative language that compiles to ARM64 at load time, and its DSP runs in that code. There are no plugins and no samples here. This score uses only built-in machines:

| Machine | Kind | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `drum2` (DS-404) | analog-style drum synth | kick, boom, clap, hats, keystroke ticks |
| `concoction` | wavetable synth with mod matrix | reese bass, pad, hum, lock blips, cut bursts, risers |
| `fm86` | DX7-style FM | the bell on `Done` |
| `sat2` | 8-mode saturator | bass grit per shot, drum and master dirt |
| `era` | sampler-era converter (rate, bits) | the crush on "— composing", the blips |
| `char2` | compressor with lo-fi stage | bit crush on ticks, bursts, clap; the lock-frame tears |
| `tape2` | tape emulation | the hum's wow, flutter, dropouts; pad warble |
| `verb2`, `delay2`, `chorus2` | space | plate hall return, ping-pong 1/16 echo, width |
| `eq2`, `geq8`, `comp2`, `bus2`, `limiter2` | mix tools | EQ on every part, 30 Hz cuts, kick sidechains, glue, limiting |

A project is a folder (`ff_tracking.slab/`) with one `project.json`: tracks, clips, notes, per-note expression, automation, routing and each machine's parameters.

### slabkit: music as a Python script

slabkit is Slab's Python library for writing projects as code. `score.py` is a program, not a recording. It:

- **Checks everything against the real machines.** slabkit reads the machine manifests from the Slab binary, so a misspelled parameter or an out-of-range value fails right away. It also takes values in real units (Hz, seconds, dB) and switches by label (`mode="FUZZ"`).
- **Builds the arrangement:** tracks, buses (`output=`, `send()`), sidechain keys (`fx("comp2", key=kick)`) and notes placed at any beat. The beats can be fractional, so a lock at 0.3 s becomes beat 0.6.
- **Writes automation.** `automate(target, (beat, value, shape)…)` covers volume, pan, any instrument parameter or any effect parameter (`"fx1:mode"`), with linear, curve or hold segments. Per-note expression does the rest: `bend()` for the bass dive, `converge()` to fold the pad chord onto one note in the collapse.
- **Renders and reports.** `song.render(stems=True)` saves the project, runs Slab headless and prints loudness, peak, crest, frequency balance and stereo correlation for the mix and for each track's stem.

### Data flow

```text
hud::events() ──► tracks ──► out/tracks.json ──┐   cuts, locks, keystrokes, collapse, Done (s)
hud::shot()   ──► camera ──► out/camera.json ──┤   per frame: zoom, box and screen position on the output
                                               ▼
                                      score/score.py (slabkit)
                       seconds × 2 = beats at 120 BPM ─► notes on the frame
                       camera values per frame ────────► pan / filter / crush automation
                                               │
                                               ▼
                            score/ff_tracking.slab/project.json
                                               │  slab --render (headless, all fy machines)
                                               ▼
                       out/pass/score.wav ─► ffmpeg: cut at 6 s, 0.25 s fade ─► out/pass/sfx.wav
                                                                                     │
                                         flat.mp4 ──► lens render ◄──────────────────┘
                                                          │
                                                          ▼
                                                  out/tracking.mp4
```

The tempo came from the picture: 15 frames per shot at 30 fps is exactly one beat at 120 BPM, so the cuts are the downbeats. The locks (frame 9 of each shot) and keystrokes (frames 1–8) are off the 16th-note grid. Those land on their exact frames as accents against it, which suits a tracker.

Most camera signals are sampled once per frame (some every second or third) into automation points:
- the tracked box's x on screen becomes pan for the blips and ticks
- the filmed screen's centre (it slides across the frame on every shot) becomes pan for the pad, riser, hum and echo
- zoom divided by zoom at the shot's cut becomes a multiplier on the bass filter cutoff and the hat tone
- the `lock` flag becomes hold steps on a lo-fi stage

None of these are hand-drawn, so changing a shot in `SCENE_LIST` and running `tools/score.sh` moves the music with it.

### The process

The score was written by Claude Code (Claude Opus) with nooga directing, in rounds:

1. **Timing.** Read `hud/src/lib.rs` (`events()`, `shot()`, `project()`), built the workspace and exported `tracks.json`. Added the `camera` bin once the brief asked for the panning to follow the lens.
2. **Sketch.** A beat grid, the bass and chords, then one sound per event type: cut, keystroke, lock, collapse, `Done`.
3. **Measure, since the model can't listen.** Each render was checked with slabkit's stem report, with per-beat RMS of every stem, and with a spectrogram that had the cuts, locks, collapse and `Done` drawn over it. That showed, for example:
   - the first version was 72% sub and nearly mono (correlation 0.99)
   - the collapse lost energy where it should build
   - giving the bass a different saturation per shot swung its level 9 dB between shots; trimming each mode's output brought it within about 1.5 dB
4. **Brief from nooga, by ear.** More grit on the bass varying by shot, louder glitches, one heavy Era moment, a transformer-hum and tape-warble bed, replacing the high melody with crushed blips on random notes of the scale, a hard cut below 30 Hz and EQ on everything. Distortion was pushed hard, with level and balance re-measured after each pass so it doesn't turn to mush.
5. **Delivery.** Limiter ceiling at -2.2 dBFS for a true peak of -1 dBTP before AAC, then the 6 s cut and fade, then their lens pass.

## Files

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `hud/src/bin/camera.rs` | New bin: per frame, zoom/tilt/roll, the tracked box's position in the 1920×1080 output (via `hud::project`), and where the flat screen's centre lands |
| `score/score.py` | The score. It reads both JSON files, writes the Slab project with Slab's Python kit (slabkit) and renders it headless |
| `score/ff_tracking.slab/project.json` | The generated Slab project (17 tracks and buses, notes, automation, effects); it opens in Slab for editing |
| `score/score.wav` | The render, cut to 6 s at 48 kHz (1.1 MB), so the video builds without Slab |
| `tools/score.sh` | `render.sh` with the score in place of `sfx.py`. Without `SLAB` it uses `score/score.wav`; with `SLAB=/path/to/slab` it renders the score again |
| `README.md` | A short "Score" paragraph under How it works, a "Slab score" section, and the layout |

## Try it

```bash
tools/score.sh                      # with the committed score.wav
SLAB=/path/to/slab tools/score.sh   # render the score again (Slab built with zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast)
```

I ran both from a clean checkout of this branch. Each builds `out/tracking.mp4`: 180 frames, 6.000 s, with audio.

Licenses: `score/score.py` imports slabkit, which is GPL-3.0 like Slab. The script, the project and the rendered WAV are offered here under this repo's MIT license.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: Slab Sounds
body: Hi @mrsarac So here is how I made https://x.com/MGasperowicz/status/2108692059431342428?s=20 ## Tools Slab, my OSS DAW with a JITed DSP engine: https://github.com/nooga/slab (It sounds better than ad-hoc synths that Claude writes, that's the whole point of it) Discord, if you're interested in chatting about it: https://discord.gg/AnF3TUwmzR ## Process Described in #1 ## Result As seen on X https://x.com/MGasperowicz/status/2108692059431342428?s=20 The Slab project project is fully editable, looks like this in the DAW: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1xElFLyGi88 I PRed you the python generator and the slab project file. ## Slab utility Making sounds: You can easily generate Slab files programmatically in any language - see `slabkit` bundled with Slab for example. The project also has production skills checked in. Slab renders audio headlessly using the exact same DSP chain as the GUI. Slab as a source: You can read Slab files and sync to them - they contain all note and automation info visible in the above YT video so it's relatively easy to sync or render visualizations from those. Slab can also render each track separately when needed. Since agents don't hear I gave them some tools to analyze and visualize audio (image below) - Claude uses these routinely to see how the project sounds, measure sonic energy in different bands etc. This data also lends itself to ad-hoc analysis in python.

title: Add Windows Vulkan rendering support
body:
The project currently assumes Metal/Apple silicon. This adds a Windows Vulkan path so the original composition can build and render on Windows, while retaining the existing macOS Metal configuration.

Changes:
- Select Vulkan for the renderer and native player on Windows, and retain Metal on non-Windows targets.
- Link Windows against a shared FFmpeg installation instead of requesting source-built codecs; retain the original codec features on macOS.
- Bound Windows GPU concurrency and frame buffering to reduce memory pressure, especially for longer compositions.
- Add a PowerShell pipeline and Windows prerequisites/setup instructions. The pipeline checks failed steps and supports a custom Cargo target directory.

Validation on Windows:
- Release build of hud, flat and lens succeeded.
- All 3 existing hud tests passed.
- Ran tools/render.ps1 end to end: track export, 4K flat pass, Python sound synthesis and final lens pass.
- ffprobe confirmed the final 6-second video has 180 frames at 1920x1080, plus a 6-second audio stream.
- Checked the aarch64-apple-darwin feature graph: Metal and the original h264/libav-agree-gpl features remain enabled. A macOS build/runtime test was not available; interactive preview was not exercised.

This contains only reusable Windows changes and documentation; no custom promo assets or machine-specific installation paths are included.

title: Port the Slab score to Rust with exact Python parity
body:
The Slab score can now be regenerated from Rust with `SLAB=/path/to/slab cargo run -p score -- --render`. The new workspace crate uses a pinned commit of the MIT-licensed [slabkit-rs](https://github.com/nooga/slabkit-rs) library; `tools/score.sh` selects it by default when re-rendering. `SCORE_IMPL=python` retains the original reference path, and the committed Python script, project and WAV are unchanged.

The Rust arrangement preserves the complete Python project, including its seeded MT19937/rejection sampling, decimal note rounding, colors, clip names, routing, expression and automation array order. An offline regression test compares every field and numeric value against the existing project: 17 tracks/buses and 249 notes. A live comparison tool runs both generators in temporary directories using the same Slab resources, including changed camera/event inputs.

Validation:
- `cargo test --locked -p score -p hud` — all six tests pass; the score tests require neither Slab nor Python.
- `cargo clippy -p score --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt -p score -- --check`, and `bash -n tools/score.sh` pass.
- `SLAB=… python3 tools/check_score.py --render` — original and altered inputs produce exactly equal JSON values and bit-for-bit identical float32 audio samples, rendered with Slab commit `b8b6566dfaa7666779bd54e4c21c5b64ef2b0e9d`.

The score remains a separately rendered WAV consumed by the existing fframes lens. Slab remains the external audio renderer. The MT19937 algorithm's BSD notice is included in `licenses/MT19937.txt`.

title: Render on Linux with Vulkan, and fall back to the CPU
body:
This makes ff-tracking build and render on Linux. The GPU path uses Vulkan, as the Windows path from #3 does, and a CPU fallback covers machines without a GPU.

**What changes**
- `flat` and `lens` use the Vulkan Skia backend on every non-macOS target. On Linux they also enable fframes' `h264`/`libav-agree-gpl` encoder features, as macOS does.
- A shared `tools/backend.rs` picks the backend from `FF_BACKEND`:
  - `auto` (default) tries the platform GPU and falls back to the CPU, printing that it did;
  - `gpu` fails if no GPU context can be created;
  - `cpu` never creates one.
- The CPU flat pass uses tiny-skia. The CPU lens pass uses Skia's raster context, so the SkSL lens shader still runs. Perspective, depth of field, palette, aberration, bloom, LED grid, tear and grain are all kept.
- `tools/render.sh` validates `FF_BACKEND`, honours `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`, and falls back to `uv run --with numpy --with scipy` when those packages are missing.
- The README lists the Linux requirements.
- `lens` gets a unit test that the lens SkSL compiles on the CPU path.

**Tested on Linux** (CachyOS, kernel 7.2, RTX 3080 Ti, NVIDIA Vulkan driver), with these results:
- `cargo test -p hud` and `cargo test --release -p flat -p lens --bins` pass.
- `FF_BACKEND=gpu tools/render.sh`: 180 frames, 30 fps, 1920x1080, 6.0 s, AAC audio. It took 117 s end to end.
- `FF_BACKEND=cpu tools/render.sh`, with every Vulkan ICD hidden: the same frame count, size and audio. It took 513 s.
  - Against the GPU master the CPU master scores SSIM 0.80 and PSNR 28.2 dB. A 12-frame contact sheet matches frame for frame; the differences are antialiasing and filter softness.
- With the Vulkan ICDs hidden, both binaries fall back to the CPU under `FF_BACKEND=auto` and fail clearly under `FF_BACKEND=gpu`.
- `rustfmt --check` is clean on the changed files. `cargo clippy --no-deps -p flat -p lens --bins -- -D warnings` reports nothing in the changed code; the only hits are two existing `is_multiple_of` lints in `flat/src/lib.rs`, which this PR doesn't touch.

**Not tested:** macOS (Metal) and Windows. Their code paths aren't meant to change, apart from the shared backend selection. `preview` still needs a GPU and a window; the fallback is for offline rendering only.

Opened as a draft. Thanks for the project, Mustafa!
